title: Aghlabid Dynasty
capsule: The Aghlabids were an Arab dynasty of the Banu Tamim tribe ruling Ifriqiya (modern Tunisia, northeastern Algeria, and Tripolitania) as nominal vassals of the Abbasid Caliphate from 800, when Harun al-Rashid appointed Ibrahim ibn al-Aghlab as hereditary emir. Their most consequential achievement was the conquest of Sicily, launched under Ziyadat Allah I in 827 and completed with the fall of Taormina in 902, alongside raids into Sardinia, Corsica, Malta, and southern Italy. They patronized major construction in Kairouan, including the Great Mosque's oldest surviving minaret in North Africa, and fostered trans-Saharan trade. The dynasty collapsed when the Ismaili Fatimid missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i led a Kutama Berber revolt that swept across Ifriqiya; the last Aghlabid ruler Ziyadat Allah III fled in 909 and the Fatimid Caliphate was proclaimed.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core territory in Ifriqiya is well-attested from Abbasid administrative records and Arab geographers; the precise boundaries of Aghlabid control in the western Maghreb and Sicily fluctuated considerably and are less certain.
